implementation_notes: EventTarget is the platform's implementation of the pattern: addEventListener(type, listener, options) subscribes, removeEventListener unsubscribes, dispatchEvent notifies synchronously with an Event object that carries the payload, and a class extending EventTarget is a subject with the registry built in. It replaces the Subject/Observer interface pair, and the options bag covers the common variations (once, passive, capture) while AbortSignal (signal: controller.signal) makes unsubscription automatic. A hand-written registry or an RxJS Observable is worth it only when filters, operators or ordering guarantees outgrow the single options bag.
pitfalls: Listeners are strongly referenced: a component that adds a listener and never calls removeEventListener or aborts its signal leaks - the classic single-page-application leak.

dispatchEvent is synchronous and re-entrant: a listener that dispatches the same event again recurses, and an exception in a listener is reported as an uncaught error instead of reaching the dispatcher.
In a normal function listener `this` is the target, while an arrow listener captures the enclosing `this`; mixing the two silently changes what the handler sees.
Event names are strings and payloads are untyped: a typo in the type string is a listener that never fires, with no error anywhere.

variants.name: node:events EventEmitter (Node runtime)
variants.implementation_notes: On the server the runtime's EventEmitter is the dominant realization: `class Subject extends EventEmitter` is the whole subject, emit(type, ...args) calls every listener synchronously in registration order, on/once/off (addListener/removeListener) are the registry operations, and an 'error' event with no listener throws. EventEmitter implements the listener list so the subject class is one line; prefer EventTarget when the same code must run in browsers too, and add a library only when typed events or operators are required.
pitfalls: Listeners are stored strongly and each emitter warns above ten listeners (setMaxListeners): repeated on() calls in a request path leak memory and multiply callbacks.
emit() invokes listeners synchronously in registration order; an async listener whose promise rejects becomes an unhandled rejection unless captureRejections is enabled.
Emitting 'error' with no listener throws from inside emit(), so error events need a default handler even when the subscriber is optional.
Passing an arrow function or an inline closure to off() removes nothing - keep the reference, or use once()/AbortSignal-free bookkeeping deliberately.
